opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that these claims have a pretty poor track record, and they're usually not specific enough to be useful. If you go back even five or six years, you'll find people confidently saying that language models will never be able to do arithmetic reliably, or never write coherent code, or never pass some reasoning benchmark, or never understand a joke. And then a couple of model generations later, those capabilities just show up, often without anyone doing anything special to target them. So when I hear a new claim of the form "language models will never do X," my prior is that it's probably going to age badly.

The deeper issue is that "never" claims are rarely tied to a mechanism that actually makes predictions. People will point to some current failure, say a model can't count the letters in a word or makes a silly mistake on a simple puzzle, and then extrapolate from that to some fundamental limitation of the architecture. But a current failure on its own doesn't tell you much about whether the limitation is fundamental or just a matter of scale, data, training method, or some fairly minor engineering fix. Unless you have a real argument for why more compute or better training can't close the gap, you're mostly just describing where the frontier is today.

What I find much more interesting are questions like: how fast are capabilities improving on a given task, what does the scaling look like, how much compute or data would it plausibly take to get a model to a certain level, and which skills seem to be lagging relative to others and why. Those are questions where you can actually look at evidence and make forecasts that might be wrong in informative ways. For example, it's genuinely interesting that models got very good at things like exam-style knowledge questions well before they got good at long-horizon agentic tasks, or at operating reliably in messy real-world environments. That tells you something about what's hard. Saying "they'll never do it" doesn't.

So it's not that I think there are no limitations. I think there clearly are important gaps right now, and some of them might take a long time to close. It's that "never" is the wrong frame. The useful question is "when, and at what cost," and claims that don't engage with that just aren't very informative.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the poor track record and lack of specificity of “never” claims, but does not identify the exclusion of chain-of-thought-scaffolded reasoning models from “language models.”

fable-5.1.text:
Mostly because they have such a bad track record. If you go back five or ten years, you can find very confident claims that language models would never do arithmetic, never do multi-step reasoning, never write working code, never understand what they're saying in any meaningful sense. And then, one by one, those things happened. So when someone tells me today that there's some specific capability that's permanently out of reach, my prior is that they're going to be wrong, and probably wrong fairly soon.

The deeper problem is that these claims usually aren't backed by any real argument. People point at a failure of the current model and treat it as evidence about the whole paradigm. But the current model is a point on a trend, not the endpoint of it. If you want to say "this will never happen," you need some account of why scaling, more data, better training methods, and architectural tweaks all fail to get you there. Almost nobody provides that. They just say "look, it can't do this," and that's not an argument about the future, it's an observation about the present.

There's also an issue with how the capabilities get defined. The claim is often something like "models will never truly understand" or "never really reason," and those words are slippery enough that the goalposts move whenever a model does the thing. If a capability can't be operationalized into a test the model could in principle pass, then the claim isn't really making a prediction, so there's nothing to engage with.

What I find much more interesting are the quantitative questions. Not "will models ever do X," but "how much compute, how much data, how long until they do X, and what does the world look like when they can." Those questions have answers you can be wrong about in measurable ways, and getting them right actually matters for how you plan. The "never" claims don't give you anything to work with, so I tend to just set them aside.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vague definitions of “understand” and “reason,” but it does not identify chain-of-thought-scaffolded reasoning models as excluded from “language models.”

astra-6.text:
Because “never” is a very strong claim, and usually what we actually care about is when. If you say language models will never be able to do something, and then a model does it two years later, that settles the question. But until then, you can keep pointing to the fact that they haven’t done it yet. That doesn’t tell us much about whether there’s a fundamental limitation or whether we just need better training or more scale.

I’d find a more specific prediction much more interesting: this capability won’t emerge in the next five years, or it won’t emerge with this amount of compute using these methods. Then we can discuss the reasons and what evidence would change our minds. The practically important question is whether these systems will acquire consequential capabilities on a timescale we need to prepare for, rather than whether there’s something they’ll be unable to do forever.

r001.rationale: The response says “never” claims are uninteresting because they are hard to falsify until a capability appears, and favors time-bounded predictions. It does not mention excluding chain-of-thought-scaffolded reasoning models from the term “language models.”

sol-6.1.text:
Because “never” is such a strong claim, and usually there isn’t a very strong argument behind it. Someone points to a thing current models can’t do and treats that as a fundamental limitation. But it’s hard to distinguish a fundamental limitation from something that goes away with more scale, better training, or a different way of using the model.

I’m more interested in quantitative questions: How much improvement would it take to get this capability? How much compute or data would you need? Could it happen in the next few years? Those questions matter even if you agree that, eventually, the capability is possible. Saying it will never happen tends to skip the part of the discussion where most of the interesting uncertainty is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about whether current models’ limitations are fundamental, but does not identify excluding chain-of-thought-scaffolded reasoning models from the definition of “language models” as a reason such claims are uninteresting.
